passage: Observation note by Usha, play-group teacher. At circle time, Imran, nearly three, called out "My truck! My truck!" while a classmate was still telling us about her kitten. He was not being unkind; he was beaming and full of news. I laid a hand flat on the mat and said, "Her turn, then your turn." He fidgeted, waited, and then told us about the truck. I will use the same words each day.

qa.q: What did Imran call out during circle time?
qa.a: He called out "My truck! My truck!" while a classmate was talking about her kitten.

qa.q: What does Imran's beaming face suggest he wants, and what else might explain the interruption?
qa.a: She reads it as eagerness, because he was beaming and full of news. It could also be that he simply could not hold the thought for long.

qa.q: What could Usha do to help the habit grow?
qa.a: She can keep repeating the same short words and pausing, and praise him when he waits even briefly. 👍

qa.q: How might the classmate with the kitten feel when she is talked over?
qa.a: She may feel cut off or hurried, so the pause for her turn matters to her as well.

grounding: A toddler talks over others because turn-taking is not yet formed, and the adult models a brief pause.

passage: At the anganwadi in the village, Salma was showing the little ones a picture of a cow when Elizabeth, two, tugged her sleeve and chattered over her. "Bird! Bird! Bird!" Salma smiled and raised one finger. "Wait, then Elizabeth's turn." She finished her sentence, turned, and said, "Now your turn. Which bird?" Elizabeth pointed at a crow on the tin roof.

qa.q: Where was Elizabeth when she interrupted?
qa.a: She was at the anganwadi in the village.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth probably feeling when she talked over Salma?
qa.a: She was probably excited by the bird and wanted to share it right away. She could also have wanted Salma's attention for herself.

qa.q: What did Salma do that helps a toddler learn turns?
qa.a: She paused with a simple gesture, said a short phrase, finished her own sentence and then gave Elizabeth a clear turn.

qa.q: What would change if Salma had scolded Elizabeth instead?
qa.a: Elizabeth might feel her excitement was wrong and share less, without having learned what to do instead.

grounding: A toddler talks over others because turn-taking is unformed, and the adult models a pause and the phrase for turns.
